{{Uniform polyhedra db|Uniform dual polyhedron stat table|lDhI|No-Face-Image=True}}
In [[geometry]], the '''small dodecahemicosacron''' is the dual of the [[small dodecahemicosahedron]], and is one of nine [[dual hemipolyhedra]]. It appears visually indistinct from the [[great dodecahemicosacron]].

Since the hemipolyhedra have [[Face (geometry)|faces]] passing through the center, the [[Dual polyhedron|dual figures]] have corresponding [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] at infinity; properly, on the [[real projective plane]] at infinity.<ref>{{Harv|Wenninger|2003|loc = [https://books.google.com/books?id=mfmzUjhs-_8C&pg=PA101 p. 101]}}</ref> In [[Magnus Wenninger]]'s ''Dual Models'', they are represented with intersecting [[prism (geometry)|prisms]], each extending in both directions to the same vertex at infinity, in order to maintain symmetry. In practice the model prisms are cut off at a certain point that is convenient for the maker. Wenninger suggested these figures are members of a new class of [[stellation]] figures, called ''stellation to infinity''. However, he also suggested that strictly speaking they are not polyhedra because their construction does not conform to the usual definitions.

Since the small dodecahemicosahedron has ten [[hexagon]]al [[Face (geometry)|faces]] passing through the model center, it can be seen as having ten [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] at infinity.

== See also ==
* [[Hemi-icosahedron]]{{snd}}The ten vertices at infinity correspond directionally to the 10 vertices of this abstract polyhedron.
